cards.title: Hedged answers win
cards.rule: Prefer the choice that says may, likely, could or some over one that states a firm fact.
cards.detail: Inference answers stay inside what the passage supports, so they often hedge. A choice that states a sure outcome, or invents a comparison with "than", usually goes beyond the passage.
cards.numbers: Hedge words in 48 of 140 right answers (34%) vs 97 of 420 wrong (23%). "than" in 21 of 140 right (15%) vs 116 of 420 wrong (28%).

cards.title: Sometimes nothing follows
cards.rule: If the facts are thin or mixed, the right completion can be "this is not conclusive" or "can't be concluded".
cards.detail: Students force a positive conclusion. In a run of questions the keyed answer says the evidence does not settle the matter, or says to be cautious.
cards.numbers: 8 of 70 in one chunk (5105ca38, a0b58ef0, 28dfc05a, 1755eaf0, 5632ffb4, d95a0bb8, 8e6a96f5, a13c1c66).

cards.title: The first sentence often decides
cards.rule: Read the setup: a definition, a rule or the earlier view in sentence 1 is needed in about 3 of 10 inference questions.
cards.detail: The words just before the blank tell you the shape of the answer, not its content. Definitions and norms from the opening line decide many Hard ones.
cards.numbers: About 19 of 70 and 21 of 70 answers needed sentence-1 content in the two chunks.

cards.title: Slot swaps
cards.rule: Check who does what: a wrong choice often keeps the passage's words but swaps the two things or reverses the relation.
cards.detail: College Board calls these "reverses" or misattributes the roles. They are built from passage words, so they feel right.
cards.numbers: Slot swaps were 23 of 210 wrong choices in one chunk (11%) and 14% of Hard wrong choices.

cards.title: Echoing helps on Easy, hurts on Hard
cards.rule: On Easy and Medium, the choice that reuses the passage's words is often right; on Hard, be suspicious of it.
cards.detail: Hard main-idea and detail answers paraphrase; the choice that copies the passage is usually a detail or a twist.
cards.numbers: Choice with the highest share of passage words is right: Easy 16 of 41 (39%), Medium 18 of 52 (35%), Hard 9 of 45 (20%); chance 25%.

cards.title: Main-idea answers keep the concession
cards.rule: Don't drop the "although" half automatically: right main-idea answers often keep it ("…except in certain circumstances").
cards.detail: The brief teaches that the weight is on the part after the turn. That is right for details; for main ideas the qualified claim is the main idea.
cards.numbers: Right main-idea answers keeping the concession: 1e85caa9, b7d51f84, 995d55fd, 70aacc03, f7bd14de, e80ba20d.

cards.title: Detail questions often need an inference
cards.rule: Beyond "According to the text", expect to combine two sentences or draw a consequence.
cards.detail: Only the plain "according to" questions are restatements. Hard detail questions never restate one sentence.
cards.numbers: 0 of 13 Hard detail questions in one chunk restate a sentence.

cards.title: Echoing the passage is a trap
cards.rule: Don't pick the choice because it repeats the most passage words.
cards.detail: In support, weaken and quotation questions the right choice tests the claim; distractors borrow the passage's nouns but test something else.
cards.numbers: Choice with the most passage words is right in 46 of 277 (17%; chance 25%); shortest choice right in 35 of 277 (13%).

cards.title: Data support = a comparison
cards.rule: For "which data support the claim", choose a choice that compares the groups the claim names.
cards.detail: A single number about one group can't show an effect. Right choices contain than/whereas/more/less/higher/lower far more often.
cards.numbers: Comparison word in 34 of 49 right "describes data" answers (69%) vs 77 of 147 wrong (52%).

cards.title: Hedged claims need the exception
cards.rule: When the claim says "not fully supported", "necessary but not sufficient" or "surprised", the right data choice reports the exception.
cards.detail: The main trend is the trap; the claim is about the case that breaks it.
cards.numbers: f8244f7c D, 24c1b7e4 D, 9452092c A, cca6fae9 D.

cards.title: Effect-size claims
cards.rule: "Moderate", "varies by", "except among", "provided that": compare how big the effect is in each condition, not the raw levels.
cards.detail: These Hard questions ask whether an effect is stronger in one condition than another.
cards.numbers: 09775cbf A, 82bdf676 B, d5b9ed0d B, 627d93e3 D.

cards.title: Swapped variables
cards.rule: Underline the two variables in the claim; the right finding relates exactly those two.
cards.detail: Hard distractors relate the right nouns in the wrong pair (complexity–fusion instead of fusion–exotericity).

cards.title: Colon or dash after the blank
cards.rule: If a colon, semicolon or dash follows the blank, the words after it define the blank.
cards.detail: About a quarter of fill-in questions put the definition right there.
cards.numbers: 58 of 221 fill-ins have a colon, semicolon or dash after the blank in its sentence.

cards.title: "Not ___" flips the clue
cards.rule: With not, less, hardly, unlikely or "need not" next to the blank, the clue describes the opposite of the answer.
cards.detail: Rare on Easy, common on Medium and Hard.
cards.numbers: Negation before the blank: Easy 2 of 110, Medium 7 of 54, Hard 5 of 57.

cards.title: A refuted view
cards.rule: After "misconception", "accepted view" or "critics asserted", the blank holds the view being overturned: the opposite of the evidence that follows.
cards.detail: The evidence comes after; the blank is what it disproves.
cards.numbers: 17 of 221 fill-ins (Easy 8, Medium 3, Hard 6).

cards.title: Meaning questions use other senses
cards.rule: In "most nearly means" questions every wrong choice is another real meaning of the word; the plain physical sense is often right.
cards.detail: Substitute each choice into the sentence: supported = held up, drew = pulled, assumed = acquired.
cards.numbers: 40 meaning questions; e.g. e3ffb854, 9671d61d, 84ece3f6.

cards.title: The longest choice is rarely right
cards.rule: Don't lean toward the longest word or phrase.
cards.detail: Length carries no meaning here, and the longest option wins less than chance.
cards.numbers: Longest choice right in 36 of 221 fill-ins (16%; chance 25%).

cards.title: Long purpose and structure choices lose
cards.rule: On purpose and structure questions, the longest, most detailed choice is usually wrong.
cards.detail: Right answers describe the job in general words; long choices pack in specifics that the passage doesn't support.
cards.numbers: Longest choice right in 3 of 29 structure and 7 of 54 purpose questions (12%; chance 25%).

cards.title: Vague nouns on Hard
cards.rule: Hard right answers often use vague words like "a certain", "a particular", "a finding".
cards.detail: The test writes the right answer abstractly so it can't be matched word for word.
cards.numbers: Vague noun in 14 of 42 Hard right answers (33%) vs 21 of 126 wrong (17%); Easy 10% vs 5%.

cards.title: Stories: name the feeling
cards.rule: In literary purpose questions, the right choice often names a feeling.
cards.detail: Stories are about what someone feels or is like; the purpose is usually to show that.
cards.numbers: Feeling word in 11 of 29 right literary purpose answers (38%) vs 20 of 87 wrong (23%).

cards.title: Stance verbs are traps
cards.rule: Be wary of purpose choices that say the author argues, urges or criticizes.
cards.detail: Most SAT passages explain or describe; strong stance verbs overstate them.
cards.numbers: Stance verb opens 3 of 54 right purpose answers (6%) vs 23 of 162 wrong (14%).

cards.title: Respond answers hedge
cards.rule: For "how would the author of Text 2 respond", prefer the choice with a limiting word (may, not necessarily, only some, overlooks).
cards.detail: Most responses qualify the other text instead of flatly agreeing or flatly rejecting.
cards.numbers: Hedge or limiting word in 22 of 42 right respond answers (52%) vs 34 of 126 wrong (27%).

cards.title: "Both agree" hides a disagreement
cards.rule: When asked what both authors agree on, expect them to disagree about something else; the shortest choice often wins.
cards.detail: The agreement is a narrow shared point, not either author's main claim.
cards.numbers: Texts disagree elsewhere in 8 of 12 agree questions; shortest choice right in 6 of 12.

cards.title: "Neither text mentions"
cards.rule: Check each choice against both texts: almost half of wrong choices bring in something neither text says.
cards.detail: These sound plausible because they stay on topic.
cards.numbers: 87 of 183 wrong choices are rejected as not in either text.

cards.title: Contrast already printed? Not another contrast
cards.rule: If the sentence before the blank already turns (however, though, but, although), the blank is usually not a contrast word.
cards.detail: The turn has been made; the next link is usually a result, an example or an emphasis.
cards.numbers: Contrast answer in 3 of 32 such questions (9%) vs 32 of 162 otherwise (20%).

cards.title: Name the family, then pick
cards.rule: Group the four choices by job (contrast, cause, support/example, addition/similarity, time). The answer's family is almost always unique.
cards.detail: You rarely need to separate "for example" from "specifically"; the bank doesn't make you.
cards.numbers: Answer family unique in 64 of 65 questions of one chunk.

cards.title: A word added in one choice is wrong
cards.rule: If only one choice adds a word (and, it, that, which, while), cross it out.
cards.detail: The test adds a word to make a choice look complete; it almost always breaks the sentence.
cards.numbers: Wrong in 46 of 47 cases bank-wide; the exception is ", but" joining two full sentences (85b8b9c5).

cards.title: "and" with no comma
cards.rule: Between two full sentences, "and" needs a comma before it. A bare "and" was never right.
cards.detail: College Board calls it a run-on or says "and" can't join the sentences this way.
cards.numbers: 0 right of 35 such choices.

cards.title: Title + name: no commas
cards.rule: A job title right before a person's name takes no commas: "biologist Yuree Lee showed".
cards.detail: The title is part of the name phrase (essential), so commas would cut it off.
cards.numbers: 7 of 7 such questions.

cards.title: Two-position questions are the Hard ones
cards.rule: When the marks change at two places, find the phrase's two edges and give them matching marks.
cards.detail: Appositives, series and adverbs like however/though are the Hard Boundaries items.
cards.numbers: Two-position questions are mostly Hard (39 of 52); adverb placement 15 of 17 Hard.

cards.title: Opener after the break
cards.rule: On Hard items the second sentence starts with an opener (Built into…, Known as…, Praising…). Find its real subject: if there is one, you need a period.
cards.detail: The opener makes the second half look like a fragment.
cards.numbers: Hard right answers with a strong break: next word is a participle or preposition in 18 of 31.

cards.title: Attractor before the blank
cards.rule: In agreement questions, the noun right before the blank often has the wrong number. Find the real subject.
cards.detail: Hard items put a long phrase between subject and verb.
cards.numbers: Opposite-number word before the blank: Easy 7 of 19, Medium 9 of 15, Hard 11 of 18.

cards.title: Simple verb form wins
cards.rule: Once you know singular or plural, take the simple form (is, was, invites), not "is being" or "have been".
cards.detail: The progressive and perfect forms are fillers in agreement questions.
cards.numbers: Simple form right in 49 of 52 agreement questions.

cards.title: Never right: it's, they're, having + -ed
cards.rule: "it's", "they're" and "having + past participle" were never the answer in the bank.
cards.detail: These are classic traps for possession and verb form.
cards.numbers: it's/they're: 0 of 15 choices; having-forms: 0 of 16 questions.

cards.title: Dangling modifier: who is doing it?
cards.rule: After an opening phrase, the next words must be the thing it describes.
cards.detail: Choices starting with "there", "it is" or a number never were right; passive "… by X" versions rarely are.
cards.numbers: There/it is/number starts: 0 of 8; passive by-phrase: 1 of 5.

cards.title: Similarity goals: no contrast word
cards.rule: If the goal is a similarity, cross out any choice with whereas, while, but, unlike or although.
cards.detail: A right similarity answer never contrasted the two items.
cards.numbers: 0 of 17 right similarity answers have a contrast word (27% of wrong choices do).

cards.title: Length depends on the goal
cards.rule: For a single fact (specify, indicate, identify), short wins; for "emphasize" goals, the fuller choice wins.
cards.detail: Fact goals want one plain sentence; emphasize goals want the feature plus its context.
cards.numbers: Fact goals: shortest right 12 of 31 (39%), longest 3 of 31 (10%). Emphasize goals: longest right 12 of 24 (50%).

cards.title: Echoing the goal is a trap
cards.rule: The choice that repeats the goal's words most is usually wrong.
cards.detail: Distractors borrow the goal's nouns but do a neighboring job.
cards.numbers: Most goal words shared: right in 27 of 204 (13%; chance 25%).

cards.title: Two-part goals
cards.rule: "Explanation and example", "duration and purpose", "make and support": the answer has both parts.
cards.detail: Each distractor gives one part only.
cards.numbers: 13f36b03 B, 54227b8e A, 0fab0c90 C, 0acc26b2 D.

flow.title: Echoing the passage is a trap that grows with difficulty
flow.rule: When a choice copies the passage's wording, check whether it actually answers the question before you take it.
flow.detail: Across the reading skills, the choice that shares the most words with the passage (or with the goal, in notes questions) is right less often than chance once questions get harder. Easy Central Ideas questions are the exception: there the echo helps.
flow.numbers: Most passage words, right answer: Command of Evidence 46 of 277 (17%); Inferences Easy 2 of 20, Medium 9 of 48, Hard 13 of 72; Central Ideas Easy 16 of 41 (39%), Medium 18 of 52 (35%), Hard 9 of 45 (20%); notes questions, most goal words 27 of 204 (13%). Chance 25%.

flow.title: Hedging marks the right answer only where the answer is a judgment
flow.rule: In inference, main-idea/detail and "how would the author respond" questions, prefer the hedged choice; elsewhere ignore hedges.
flow.detail: Bank-wide, cautious words looked useless because the reading skills were pooled. Split by skill, hedges (may, likely, could, some, not necessarily) favour the right answer in Inferences, Central Ideas and Cross-Text respond questions, but not in Command of Evidence or Text Structure.
flow.numbers: Right vs wrong choices with a hedge: Inferences 48/140 (34%) vs 97/420 (23%); Central Ideas 30/138 (22%) vs 55/414 (13%); Cross-Text respond 22/42 (52%) vs 34/126 (27%); Command of Evidence 20/277 (7%) vs 71/831 (9%); Text Structure 13/149 (9%) vs 25/447 (6%).

flow.title: Comparisons: a trap in inference, the answer in data questions
flow.rule: If the passage never compares two things, drop the choice that does; if the claim is about an effect, pick the choice that compares.
flow.detail: "than" in a choice usually signals an invented comparison in Inferences and Central Ideas. In Command of Evidence data questions the opposite holds: the right choice compares the groups the claim is about.
flow.numbers: "than": Inferences right 21/140 (15%) vs wrong 116/420 (28%); Central Ideas 11/138 (8%) vs 58/414 (14%). Comparison words in "describes data" answers: right 34/49 (69%) vs wrong 77/147 (52%).

flow.title: Length cues depend on the skill
flow.rule: Never pick by length alone, but distrust the longest choice in purpose, structure and word questions, and the shortest in evidence questions.
flow.detail: Pooled, the longest and shortest choices look like chance. By skill they are not: long choices lose in Words in Context, purpose/structure and Inferences; short choices lose in Command of Evidence; in notes questions length depends on the goal.
flow.numbers: Longest right: Words in Context fill-ins 36/221 (16%), structure 3/29 and purpose 7/54 (12%), Inferences 24/140 (17%). Shortest right: Command of Evidence 35/277 (13%). Notes: fact goals shortest 12/31 (39%), emphasize goals longest 12/24 (50%). Chance 25%.

flow.title: Medium and Hard add a flip next to the blank
flow.rule: When a "not", "hardly", "unlikely", "however" or a plural/singular noun sits next to the blank, slow down and invert or skip it.
flow.detail: Several skills get harder in the same way: a negation or reversal sits right beside the decision point, so the clue has to be inverted. Word questions add "not ___"; Transitions put a contrast in the sentence before; grammar questions place an opposite-number noun right before the verb.
flow.numbers: Negation before a word blank: Easy 2/110, Medium 7/54, Hard 5/57. Opposite-number word before an agreement blank: Easy 7/19, Medium 9/15, Hard 11/18. Contrast already before a transition blank: contrast answer in 3/32 vs 32/162.

flow.title: The deciding words are often away from the blank
flow.rule: After reading around the blank, scan the first sentence and the sentence after the blank for a definition, a rule or a restatement.
flow.detail: The site teaches "look at the words just before the blank". That gives the form of the answer, but the content often comes from elsewhere: a definition or rule in sentence 1 for Inferences, a following sentence for word questions, an opened dash or comma pair for Boundaries.
flow.numbers: Inferences needing sentence-1 content: about 19 of 70 and 21 of 70 in the two chunks. Word fill-ins with a later sentence: Easy 31/110, Medium 9/54, Hard 19/57.

flow.title: Hard right answers are worded abstractly
flow.rule: On Hard purpose, structure and main-idea questions, a general-sounding choice that fits the logic beats a concrete one that copies details.
flow.detail: On Hard questions the right choice tends to describe the passage in general terms (a certain claim, a particular finding, a consideration) while wrong choices keep concrete passage nouns.
flow.numbers: Vague nouns in Hard Text Structure right answers 14/42 (33%) vs 21/126 wrong (17%). Central Ideas Hard: passage-word echo right 9/45 (20%).

flow.title: Wrong choices do a neighbouring job
flow.rule: Ask "does it do what the question asks?" before "is it true?".
flow.detail: In notes, evidence and purpose questions the most common wrong choice is accurate but does a different job: the aim instead of the finding, one item instead of both, a true fact about the wrong group, an example instead of the generalization.
flow.numbers: Notes: about 439 of 612 wrong-choice explanations say the choice "doesn't" do the goal (brief). Similarity goals: contrast word in 0/17 right vs 14/51 wrong. Aim goals: result words in 1/9 right vs 7/27 wrong.

flow.title: No answer-letter pattern
flow.detail: Answer letters are close to even across the 1,845 Reading and Writing questions; the small leans within skills (B in Words in Context, D in Transitions) are too weak to use.
flow.numbers: All RW: A 462, B 457, C 434, D 492. Words in Context B 80 of 261 (31%); Transitions D 59 of 194 (30%).

fix.was: Picking the careful-sounding choice. Cautious words (may, some, often, likely) appear in 29.6% of correct choices and 27.5% of wrong ones.
fix.now: Pooling hides a real signal. Hedges favour the right answer in Inferences (34% vs 23%), Central Ideas (22% vs 13%) and Cross-Text respond questions (52% vs 27%); they do nothing in Command of Evidence (7% vs 9%).
fix.ev: Inferences 48/140 vs 97/420; Central Ideas 30/138 vs 55/414; CTC respond 22/42 vs 34/126; COE 20/277 vs 71/831.

fix.was: Picking the choice that repeats the passage. Of 571 questions, the right answer had the highest share of passage words in 126 and the lowest in 121, about what chance gives.
fix.now: The average hides opposite effects: the echo helps on Easy and Medium Central Ideas (39%, 35%) and is a trap in Command of Evidence (17%), Hard Central Ideas (20%) and Inferences (17–19% on Medium/Hard).
fix.ev: Unique highest-overlap choice right: COE 46/277; CID E 16/41, M 18/52, H 9/45; INF M 9/48, H 13/72.

fix.was: Picking by length. The correct choice is the longest of the four in 19% of questions and the shortest in 17%. Chance is about 25%.
fix.now: True pooled, but skill-specific cues are usable as tie-breakers: longest right only 12% in purpose/structure and 16% in word fill-ins; shortest right only 13% in Command of Evidence; in notes questions the shortest wins 39% of single-fact goals.
fix.ev: Structure 3/29, purpose 7/54; WIC 36/221; COE 35/277; RS fact goals 12/31.

fix.was: How inference wrong choices fail: Not in the passage 62%, Opposite 32%, Twisted or too strong 3%, Misses the job 3%.
fix.now: Reading every wrong choice's explanation, about half are new material, but about a quarter are built from passage words: slot swaps, too strong, misplaced detail, half right. Slot swaps alone are 14% of Hard wrong choices.
fix.ev: Chunk inf-1: new material 48%, contradicts 21%, passage-word builds 24%, logic misfire 7% (of 210). Chunk inf-2: passage-based archetypes 49/210 (23%).

fix.was: Look first at the words just before the blank; the answer rests on the Found or Did lines before it in 36 of 42.
fix.now: The words before the blank fix the form of the answer, but about 3 in 10 answers need sentence-1 content (a definition, rule or the earlier view).

fix.was: After suggesting that or therefore: what follows.
fix.now: In 8 of 70 questions the right completion is that nothing firm follows ("is not conclusive evidence", "it can't be concluded", "exercise caution").

fix.was: Main idea: No sentence can be skipped: the answer has to cover the whole passage.
fix.now: The answer usually rests on one claim sentence and leaves out examples and background.

fix.was: Detail: the answer restates what is said there.
fix.now: Only plain "According to the text" questions restate; 0 of 13 Hard detail questions in one chunk restate a sentence.

fix.was: "Although X, Y." The weight is on Y; X is true but is not the point.
fix.now: Right for details, overstated for main ideas: right main-idea answers often keep the concession.
fix.ev: 1e85caa9 A, b7d51f84 A, 995d55fd A, 70aacc03 C, f7bd14de D, e80ba20d A.

fix.was: however or though already printed in the sentence before the blank's sentence: the blank is a result word in 8.
fix.now: The safe rule is "not a contrast word": with but, although or a same-sentence however, the answer can be an example, a specific detail, emphasis or a final step.
fix.ev: Bank-wide, a contrast word in the sentence(s) before the blank leaves a contrast answer in only 3 of 32 questions; non-result answers include d3898d32 (Specifically), feb1e6da (in fact), 332e75bf (Ultimately), 827afb27 (example).

fix.was: Four choices, four different jobs: in more than half the questions, naming the link leaves exactly one choice.
fix.now: Understated. Grouping example/specifically/in fact as one support family, the answer's family is unique in 64 of 65 questions of one chunk.

fix.was: 17.2 "Matching frames: In X, … ____ in Y" presented as a similarity signal.
fix.now: The frame shows parallel structure, not direction: 221ecf0f has that frame and its answer is "by contrast".

fix.was: A fragment is a period in front of words that cannot stand alone.
fix.now: College Board also names the opener before the period as the fragment.

fix.was: Rule 1.7 frames 5aa1fffd as direct versus reported question.
fix.now: Neither statement-order choice is grammatical; the item tests that "where" needs an auxiliary.

fix.was: When the goal is a similarity (17), it has both, like, also or similar in 82%, against 16%.
fix.now: Stronger rule: no right similarity answer contains a contrast word (0 of 17), while 14 of 51 wrong choices do.

fix.was: Find the clue in the blank's own sentence.
fix.now: Usually right, but in 59 of 221 fill-ins another sentence follows the blank, and it often holds the clue (a restating noun, an example, the evidence that refutes a view).

fix.was: Choice text in a few Boundaries questions contains the next choice's letter (export artifact), e.g. "2 B. 200,000 km , Puntland Desert".
fix.now: Superscripts (km², ¹³C) broke loose in the export, so choices B–D carry a stray number and letter. The answer key is unaffected.

fix.was: Explanation for 2df56712 quotes text that is not in the passage.
fix.now: The rationale quotes "very little of what she and Rachel Elkind composed … was used"; the passage says "almost all the music … was unused". Written for an earlier passage version; key unaffected.

fix.was: Skill labels that do not fit the question.
fix.now: 5eda42a3 (purpose of a poem) and 5869a196 (which question would test validity) are filed as Central Ideas and Details; dbbbc5dd, d748c3fd, 7a895def are function questions filed as Inferences.
